statement: In adults entering one US residential research unit to come off opioids, 30 people whose urine showed fentanyl (enrolled 2021 to 2024) compared with 103 people who entered about a decade earlier with other opioids such as heroin (2010 to 2015), all given the same fixed morphine treatment (only the fentanyl cohort could also have other medicines for symptoms), were associated with more withdrawal while on that treatment: their self-rated withdrawal rose to a peak in the first days and then eased, while the earlier group's fell steadily from the first day; on four of the days severe self-rated withdrawal was 3 to 6 times as common (for example 47% against 8%); observers rated most of the fentanyl group as mildly withdrawn on most days against a small minority of the earlier group, though almost no one in either group was rated above moderate; and 43% against 19% had a fast heart rate at least once. Anxiety, aches, stomach symptoms, sweating and many other symptoms were all higher, with no single symptom explaining the difference. The comparison group came from another decade and another trial, the fentanyl group was older and could be given extra comfort medicines, ratings were not blind, and xylazine and other adulterants were not tested, so fentanyl cannot be shown to be the cause; the study also measured withdrawal during morphine treatment, not untreated withdrawal. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: People coming off illicit fentanyl in one research unit had worse withdrawal than people coming off heroin there ten years earlier, even though both got the same medicine. Their withdrawal got worse over the first days before easing, and fast heartbeats were more common. Because the two groups were from different times and the fentanyl group got extra medicines, we cannot be sure fentanyl itself caused the difference.
population: Adults with opioid use disorder entering a residential research unit in Baltimore for withdrawal management within two randomized trials; 133 people, 84% men, 56% Black
comparator: Urine positive for other opioids, no fentanyl, at entry about a decade earlier (2010 to 2015), with the same fixed morphine treatment on the same unit
outcome: Self-rated (SOWS) and observer-rated (COWS) withdrawal, its course over the stabilization days, heart rate, blood pressure and pupil size
magnitude: No effect sizes or confidence intervals reported. Severe self-rated withdrawal, fentanyl against earlier cohort: 48% against 16%, 47% against 8%, 37% against 6% and 27% against 6% on four consecutive days; observer-rated mild withdrawal 73% against 33% up to 73% against 18% on the following days; tachycardia at least once 43% against 19% (p < 0.05). Peak self-rated scores higher on five of seven days (SOWS model F(1,6) = 12.44, p < 0.01); observer-rated on six of seven days (F(1,6) = 7.76, p < 0.001); the abstract gives one day fewer for each.

evidence.locator: Results › Self-Reported Withdrawal (SOWS) › Total Peak Scores, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Peak self-rated withdrawal differed by cohort, day and their interaction (F(1,6) = 12.44, p < 0.01): higher in the Fentanyl cohort from the second to the sixth stabilization day, with an inverted-U course that peaked on the second day and returned to the earlier cohort's level by the last day, while the Non-Fentanyl cohort declined steadily from the first day.

evidence.locator: Results › Self-Reported Withdrawal (SOWS) › Withdrawal Categorical Ratings, 1st paragraph; Individual Symptom Ratings, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Severe self-rated withdrawal in the Fentanyl against the Non-Fentanyl cohort: 48% against 16%, 47% against 8%, 37% against 6% and 27% against 6% on the second to fifth days; first and last days did not differ. Anxiety, sweating, tearing, runny nose, goosebumps, shaking, flushes, aches, restlessness, nausea, vomiting, twitching and stomach cramps all showed cohort, day and interaction effects; no single symptom drove the difference.

evidence.locator: Results › Observed Withdrawal (COWS) › Total Peak Scores, 1st paragraph; Withdrawal Categorical Ratings, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Peak observer-rated withdrawal higher in the Fentanyl than in the Non-Fentanyl cohort from the second to the seventh day (F(1,6) = 7.76, p < 0.001). No participant reached moderately severe or severe COWS scores; mild observer-rated withdrawal, Fentanyl against Non-Fentanyl cohort, 73% against 33%, 70% against 13%, 73% against 18%, 60% against 15%, 53% against 18% and 40% against 14% on those days.

evidence.locator: Methods › Measures, 2nd paragraph; Results › Physiological Measures › Heart Rate, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Tachycardia (heart rate above 100 at least once) in 43% of the Fentanyl cohort against 19% of the Non-Fentanyl cohort (p < 0.05); heart rate rose more steeply over the week in the Fentanyl than in the Non-Fentanyl cohort (interaction p = 0.007).

evidence.locator: Results › Participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Methods › Concomitant Medications, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The Fentanyl cohort was older than the Non-Fentanyl cohort (mean 46.0, SD 10.1, against 41.2, SD 10.2; p = 0.021). Concomitant medicines for withdrawal symptoms were available during stabilization only in the Fentanyl trial, because of uncontrolled withdrawal.

The authors list as limitations the decade between cohorts, morphine possibly stabilizing people exposed to fentanyl poorly, incomplete urine confirmation in the earlier cohort, possible xylazine in the fentanyl supply, observers not necessarily blind to exposure, the small Fentanyl group, and possible nitazenes or other synthetic opioids.

risk_of_bias.note: Historical comparison group from another trial and decade, age difference, concomitant medicines in one cohort only, unblinded ratings, no adjustment (ROBINS-E high on the card).

indirectness.note: Withdrawal measured during fixed morphine treatment, not untreated withdrawal; one US city's supply at one time.

imprecision.note: 30 people in the fentanyl cohort; no effect sizes or intervals.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; each of risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision would rate it down, so certainty is very low. Worded as an association: the design cannot separate fentanyl from era, adulterants and trial differences. Status single study.
